strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem (memorization in T2I diffusion models) and positions the contribution clearly within the three-way taxonomy of training-time, unlearning, and inference-time mitigation.

The empirical analysis in Section 5.1/Figure 1 is a genuine contribution: the finding that template memorization does not concentrate attention on EOT (unlike verbatim memorization) explains *why* the prior state of the art (Ren et al., 2024) fails on template memorization (SD v2.0: 0.356 vs. their 0.193), providing new understanding rather than just a new method.

The dynamic, per-prompt spike detector (Z-score thresholding over max attention mass) is a sensible, well-motivated generalization of hard-coded EOT attention redistribution, and the ablations (U-Net blocks, heads, timesteps, alternative attract components) are thorough and transparent.

The evaluation is careful in several respects: separate reporting for verbatim vs. template memorization, filtering to genuinely memorized prompts (SSCD > 0.7) with justification, a principled hyperparameter selection protocol with quality constraints, plus results under the traditional protocol (Figure 11) for comparability, confidence intervals, runtime comparison (Table 5), and a robustness check on non-memorized prompts (Table 3) that removes the need to know which prompts are memorized.
The limitations and impact statements are honest and specific (e.g., inference-time methods cannot protect against white-box adversaries), rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: The GUARD framework itself is technically thin: Eq. 5 is a linear combination of noise predictions (repulsion from the conditional prediction plus attraction toward a modified conditional), which is a fairly standard contrastive/negative-prompting construction. The spike detector is simple z-score thresholding, and attenuation is multiplicative logit scaling. Novelty rests mostly on the empirical analysis and engineering of the pipeline.

Scope of evaluation is limited: only SD v1.4 and SD v2.0 on Webster's 500-prompt benchmark, filtered down to 72/143/96 prompts, with 4 images per prompt. No newer architectures (SDXL, SD3, Flux) are tested, so the claim that CA-in-GUARD is 'by far the most robust method' may not generalize to modern T2I models.

Hyperparameters are tuned per architecture-memorization setting for every method (Table 2), and the 'best achievable metric' analysis effectively reports an oracle over hyperparameter configurations. While this is applied symmetrically to baselines, it makes practical deployment behavior harder to gauge and favors methods with more tunable knobs; the 15% CLIP-degradation allowance is somewhat arbitrary.

Template memorization mitigation remains incomplete: even with CA-in-GUARD, SSCD on SD v1.4 template memorization is 0.517 (vs. 0.776 no mitigation), and plain CA attenuation has a notable FID cost on SD v2.0 template memorization (245.9 vs. 188.9 for Wen et al.), which the GUARD wrapper recovers only partially (212.7).
The claimed framework/instantiation separation adds length but little substance: only one positive target is concretely developed, and the 'abstract framework' amounts to one equation.

Evaluation relies on SSCD both to select memorized prompts and as the primary mitigation metric, introducing some circularity; human evaluation or alternative similarity metrics for the near-duplicate notion would strengthen the memorization claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem (inference-time memorization mitigation in T2I diffusion models) where deployment-friendly solutions have real value.

The empirical analysis distinguishing verbatim vs. template memorization is genuinely informative: the observation that EOT-only cross-attention attenuation (Ren et al., 2024) is counterproductive for template memorization (Figure 1b/1d) provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for that method's failure and motivates the per-prompt spike detector.

The evaluation is unusually thorough: three settings (SD v1.4 verbatim/template, SD v2.0 template), multiple metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID), Pareto frontier analyses (Figure 11), ablations over U-Net blocks, attention heads, and timesteps (A.5-A.7), runtime comparison (Table 5), and a check that CA attenuation does not harm non-memorized prompts (Table 3, A.3).

The paper is transparent about its protocol choices (filtering to SSCD > 0.7, the 15% CLIP degradation budget), reports both its new protocol and the traditional one of prior work, and includes an honest limitations section acknowledging that inference-time methods do not remove memorized information from weights and cannot protect against white-box adversaries.
Strong reproducibility signals: hyperparameter search ranges are given (Table 2), the batched three-stream forward pass is described, and code availability is stated.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core ingredients are assembled from prior work: the repulsion term is essentially negative prompting / contrastive CFG arithmetic applied to the memorized prompt, and the CA attenuation builds directly on Ren et al. (2024), replacing their fixed EOT/BOT rule with a statistical outlier threshold (a z-score with tau ~3). The resulting mechanism (scale down logits of top-k spiky tokens) is a simple heuristic wrapper around an existing idea.

The central 'dominates across settings' claim is contradicted by the paper's own Table 1. Under best-SSCD configuration, CA-in-GUARD (0.517) is outperformed by Han et al. (2025) (0.479) on SD v1.4 template memorization, ties with plain CA attenuation on SD v2.0 (0.193 vs 0.193), and Wen et al. (2024) is within noise on SD v1.4 verbatim (0.115 vs 0.079, with overlapping trade-off behavior in Figure 11). 'By far the most robust method' is an overstatement; the honest conclusion is that GUARD is competitive and often best, not uniformly superior.

Quality preservation is weaker than advertised. Under the best-SSCD configuration, CLIP drops from 0.346 to 0.266 on verbatim memorization (~23% degradation) and FID gains are inconsistent; the 15% CLIP degradation budget is generous, and no human or visual evaluation substantiates that 'quality' is actually maintained. The claim that the attraction term 'boosts quality' rests on FID computed from only ~72-143 prompts x 4 images (~300-600 images), a sample size far too small for reliable FID estimation.

A significant evaluation gap: A.3 tests the safety of CA attenuation (r=0) on non-memorized prompts, but never tests full GUARD (with the repulsion term) on non-memorized inputs. Since the paper's pitch is that mitigation can be applied universally without knowing which prompts are memorized, the effect of aggressive repulsion (r up to 6.0 on SD v2.0) on benign generations is unaddressed and could be harmful.

Hyperparameter treatment raises fairness concerns: grid searches are run per setting with setting-specific ranges (e.g., r in [2.0, 6.0] only for SD v2.0), and it is unclear that baselines received an equally intensive per-metric tuning effort, particularly Han et al. (2025), the strongest competitor on template memorization.

Presentation issues: Figure 2/3/10/11 are small, multi-panel, and hard to read; Table 1 duplicates Table 4a verbatim, wasting space; the 'positive target' framing is confusing since the target is a noise prediction, not an image, and the rationale for why repelling from a noise prediction steers away from the memorized image is only sketched heuristically with no theoretical grounding.

The template-memorization results on SD v1.4 remain weak across all methods (best SSCD ~0.48-0.52 from a 0.776 start), which the paper acknowledges but does not resolve; the contribution therefore only partially addresses the hardest regime it identifies.

strengths: The empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns (Figure 1) is genuinely informative: the finding that template memorization does not rely on the EOT spike (unlike verbatim memorization) explains why hard-coded EOT attenuation (Ren et al., 2024) fails on SD v2.0, and it motivates the method in a principled way.

The per-prompt, on-the-fly spike detector (Z-score outlier detection over token attention mass) is a sensible and novel improvement over prior hard-coded trigger-token strategies, and the ablations over U-Net blocks, attention heads, and timesteps (A.5-A.7) are thorough and well-motivated.

The evaluation is one of the more careful in this literature: results are separated by memorization type and architecture, only highly-memorized examples (SSCD > 0.7) are retained to avoid inflated mitigation scores, the 'best achievable' protocol is complemented by the traditional Pareto-frontier protocol (A.8.2), baselines are re-tuned under the same protocol, and the appendix includes a robustness check on non-memorized prompts (A.3) showing the method does not harm benign generations.

Honest limitations discussion: the authors clearly state that inference-time mitigation does not remove memorized information from the weights and cannot defend against white-box adversaries, and that only black-box threat models are addressed.
Runtime measurements are reported, showing the methods are competitive in efficiency with prior inference-time approaches.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The GUARD formula (Eq. 5) is essentially standard negative-prompt/contrastive CFG: repulsion from the memorized prompt is a negative prompt, and the attraction term simply replaces the conditional. The main technical novelty reduces to the statistical spike detector plus multiplicative logit attenuation, an incremental delta over Ren et al. (2024).

Some central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Table 1 shows Han et al. (2025) achieves better SSCD than CA-in-GUARD in SD v1.4 template memorization (0.479 vs 0.517), so 'CA-in-GUARD dominates across settings' and 'by far the most robust method' are not strictly supported; also, for SD v1.4 template memorization all methods leave substantial residual memorization (0.776 -> ~0.5), which is a weak mitigation result that receives limited discussion.

The experimental scope is narrow: only two older Stable Diffusion versions (v1.4 and v2.0) are evaluated, with verbatim memorization restricted to SD v1.4; no more modern architectures (SDXL or later) are tested, which limits external validity of the 'across architectures' claim.

Quality in the template-memorization settings is poor for all methods, including the proposed one (CLIP ~0.18 vs a no-mitigation reference of ~0.22 and pretraining reference 0.299-0.323). The 15%-degradation tolerance is a lenient choice, and FID is computed on small generation sets (72-143 prompts, 4 images each) where it is statistically fragile.

The 'best achievable per metric' protocol involves a grid search over multiple hyperparameters per method per setting, selecting the best configuration on the same evaluation set being reported; this risks overfitting hyperparameters to the evaluation set and may favor methods with larger hyperparameter search spaces over simpler baselines.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the Code line in Appendix A.2 reads 'available at:' with no link, and while hyperparameter ranges are given (Table 2), key details such as how heads/blocks statistics are aggregated and the exact 'hot heads' selection are spread across prose.

The GUARD framework contribution (Section 4) is largely a repackaging of contrastive guidance; the paper would be stronger if framed primarily as the CA-attenuation method with GUARD as an ablation-level variant, rather than presenting the framework as a first-class contribution.

strengths: The empirical analysis in Section 5.1 is a genuine contribution: the observation that EOT-only cross-attention attenuation works for verbatim memorization but is counterproductive for template memorization (Figure 1) is a new insight that explains prior methods' failures and motivates the dynamic per-prompt spike detection.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: three architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0, v3.0 — including the first reported mitigation evaluation on SD v3.0), both verbatim and template memorization, three metrics, ablations over blocks/heads/timesteps/samplers/CFG scales, DINO-based retrieval metrics, full-spectrum (all 500 prompts) evaluation, non-memorized prompt robustness (Table 3), and efficiency measurements (Table 8).

The proposed evaluation protocol improvements (filtering to SSCD > 0.7 highly-memorized prompts, reporting per-metric best configurations within quality constraints) are well-motivated and transparently disclosed, with results under the traditional protocol also reported (Figure 13).
Efficiency results are favorable: CA attenuation has near-zero overhead and CA-in-GUARD is competitive with baselines in wall-clock time and memory (Table 8).
Honest limitations discussion (A.1) correctly identifies the inherent scope of inference-time mitigation (no protection under white-box threat models), and an impact statement is included.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: GUARD's repulsion term is essentially CFG with the memorized prompt as a negative prompt, and the positive target is an attention-attenuated variant of the same conditioning — ideas closely related to existing negative-prompting and prior attention-redistribution work (Ren et al., 2024). The spike detector itself is a simple Z-score threshold (τ > 3) applied per prompt. The paper's contribution is more empirical/incremental than conceptual, which should be reflected in the framing.

Evidence of overclaiming: the abstract claims the method is 'by far the most robust method... consistently producing state-of-the-art results', yet on SD v1.4 template memorization (the setting with the most prompts, n=143), Han et al. (2025) achieves a better best-SSCD (0.479 vs 0.530/0.517) and a slightly better SSCD-CLIP trade-off (A.7.2 admits this). The 'dominates across settings' claim is not fully supported.

Potential test-set contamination in hyperparameter selection: hyperparameters (τ, α, r) are grid-searched separately per architecture-memorization setting, but it is not stated whether this selection uses the same evaluation prompts on which results are reported. Given the notably different ranges per setting (e.g., r ∈ [2.0, 6.0] only for SD v2.0 template), tuning on the reported benchmark is plausible, which would favor their method over baselines relative to a held-out selection protocol.

Some quality claims are weaker than stated: CLIP scores of CA-in-GUARD are lower than plain CA attenuation in two of three main settings (Table 1), and CLIP confidence intervals are wide (e.g., ±0.015 for CA-in-GUARD), so several 'improvement or comparable' claims about quality are within noise and not statistically established.

Reproducibility gap: the Code section says 'The code for reproducing the results is available at:' but the link is empty/missing in the submitted manuscript. Given the many implementation-sensitive details (which blocks/heads, batching of three streams, in-place logit modification), the missing artifact weakens reproducibility.

The GUARD framework is introduced as a general framework with multiple possible instantiations, but the ablation of alternative attract components (A.4) is narrow (only CA-attenuation vs. semantic paraphrasing), so the generality of the framework is not well established — the paper effectively delivers one method rather than a validated framework.

FID is computed only against a 10k LAION reference set on very small generation sets (72-143 prompts × 4 images), where FID estimates are known to be high-variance; the differences in FID across methods (e.g., 212.240 vs 210.983) should be interpreted cautiously.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper tests across three settings (SD v1.4 verbatim, SD v1.4 template, SD v2.0 template) plus a SD v3.0 evaluation in the appendix, with multiple metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID, DINO retrieval), Pareto-frontier analyses, and extensive ablations (blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, CFG scales, schedulers).

The empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns distinguishing verbatim vs. template memorization (Figure 1) is a genuinely useful observation that explains why EOT-only attenuation (Ren et al., 2024) fails for template memorization, and motivates the per-prompt spike detector.

The finding that CA attenuation is robust on non-memorized prompts (Section A.3, Table 3) relaxes a common assumption of prior work (needing to know which prompts are memorized), which strengthens the practical value of the approach.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (A.1): the paper clearly acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not remove memorized information from weights and cannot protect against white-box adversaries.

Reasonable treatment of evaluation protocol: the paper explicitly discusses why filtering to highly memorized examples matters and reports results under both their protocol and the traditional Pareto-front protocol of prior work, plus full-spectrum evaluation over all 500 examples (Table 7).
Efficiency analysis (Table 8) shows the method has competitive wall-clock time and memory usage relative to baselines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core techniques are relatively simple incremental extensions of prior work. The spike detector is a straightforward per-token z-score outlier threshold on attention mass, and attenuation is a multiplicative logit scaling; the GUARD guidance (Eq. 5) is essentially negative-prompt/contrastive CFG with a modified positive target, closely related to Ren et al. (2024) and standard negative-guidance ideas. There is no theoretical analysis of why attraction-repulsion works.

Headline claims of consistent state-of-the-art are somewhat overstated: in Table 1, Han et al. (2025) actually achieves better SSCD than CA-in-GUARD on SD v1.4 template memorization (0.479 vs. 0.517), and Wen et al. achieves better FID on SD v2.0 in the best-CLIP configuration. The 'by far the most robust method' framing is stronger than the mixed evidence.

The 'best achievable per-metric' evaluation protocol (selecting each method's best configuration per metric within a 15% CLIP degradation band) is nonstandard and could favor methods with more hyperparameters; while the paper also reports Pareto frontiers, baseline hyperparameter search effort (Table 2 only covers the authors' methods) is not equally documented for baselines, raising fairness concerns.

Several design choices feel ad hoc and are justified only empirically: excluding late up-blocks, aggregating over heads/blocks, applying attenuation to all heads, the 15% degradation threshold, and per-setting hyperparameter ranges that differ substantially (Table 2). This raises generalization and overfitting-to-benchmark concerns.

The framework contribution (GUARD) is presented as a major contribution but is a fairly thin abstraction: Eq. 5 is two extra guidance terms, and the ablation of alternative positive targets (A.4) is limited to paraphrased prompts.

The improvement margins in some settings are modest relative to the added complexity (e.g., SD v1.4 template: 0.517 vs. 0.479 for the best prior method), and confidence intervals on SSCD differences between methods are not directly compared for statistical significance.
The code availability statement in Section A.2 is incomplete (the URL is blank in the manuscript), which weakens reproducibility as submitted.

strengths: Comprehensive and unusually thorough evaluation: three architectures (SD v1.4, v2.0, v3.0), both verbatim and template memorization, three metrics (SSCD, CLIP, FID), complementary DINO retrieval metrics, full-spectrum evaluation beyond the high-memorization subset, robustness ablations across samplers/steps/schedules/CFG scales, and efficiency measurements.

The empirical analysis of cross-attention patterns (Figure 1) is a genuine contribution in itself: it explains why prior EOT-only attenuation (Ren et al., 2024) fails for template memorization, and motivates the per-prompt statistical spike detector, which is a sensible and well-justified generalization of hard-coded EOT suppression.

The improved evaluation protocol (filtering to genuinely memorized prompts with SSCD > 0.7, and reporting verbatim vs. template memorization separately) is well-motivated and reveals issues in prior work's reported numbers; the paper also transparently reports results under the traditional protocol for comparability.

The method requires no prior knowledge of which prompts are memorized (Table 3 shows no degradation on non-memorized prompts), and the batched three-pass implementation keeps overhead modest (Table 8).
Honest and clear limitations section explicitly acknowledging the white-box threat model limitation of all inference-time mitigation approaches; impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: The GUARD framework itself is a fairly straightforward extension of classifier-free guidance (adding a repulsion term and a second conditional term); the conceptual novelty is moderate, with the main contribution being the CA spike detector and the empirical findings.

Hyperparameter tuning protocol raises fairness questions: grid search ranges are specified for the proposed methods (Table 2) but it is not fully specified whether baselines received an equally extensive per-setting search; the 'best achievable per metric' selection also favors methods with many tunable knobs, though the authors do report trade-off and Pareto analyses to mitigate this.

Evaluations rest on relatively small subsets (72-143 prompts, 4 generations each) after filtering, so some comparisons (e.g., CA attenuation 0.193 vs. CA-in-GUARD 0.193 on SD v2.0) have overlapping confidence intervals and the statistical significance of some gaps is unclear.

Quality costs are non-trivial in the strongest mitigation regime: e.g., CLIP drops from 0.346 (no mitigation) to 0.266 (CA-in-GUARD) on verbatim memorization; the paper is transparent about this but the headline 'state-of-the-art' claim should be read with the trade-offs in mind.
The code availability statement is incomplete in the manuscript ('The code for reproducing the results is available at:' with no link), which weakens reproducibility as submitted.

Some mechanistic claims (e.g., that spikes cause memorization, that the attraction term relieves 'pressure' on the attenuation mechanism) are supported by correlations and hypothesis-level discussion rather than causal evidence.
